content: Sorbitol, also known as glucitol, is a sugar alcohol with a sweet taste that is metabolized slowly by the human body. It is produced by the reduction of glucose, where the aldehyde group is converted into a hydroxyl group. Sorbitol is primarily derived from corn syrup but is also naturally present in fruits such as apples, pears, peaches, and prunes. It is enzymatically converted into fructose by sorbitol-6-phosphate 2-dehydrogenase. Sorbitol is an isomer of mannitol, another sugar alcohol, differing only in the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon 2. Despite their similarities, sorbitol and mannitol have distinct natural sources, melting points, and applications. Sorbitol is widely used as a sugar substitute and may be listed as an inactive ingredient in various food products. Its INS and E number is 420. Sorbitol has about 60% of the sweetness of sucrose and provides 6 kilocalories per gram, compared to the average 4 kilocalories per gram for carbohydrates. It is commonly found in diet foods, sugar-free chewing gum, mints, cough syrups, and ice cream. Sorbitol also occurs naturally in many stone fruits and berries, particularly those from the genus Sorbus. Sorbitol can act as a non-stimulant laxative when administered orally or as an enema. It exerts its laxative effect by drawing water into the large intestine, thereby promoting bowel movements. However, like other sugar alcohols, excessive consumption of sorbitol can cause gastrointestinal distress. It is considered safe for use in elderly individuals but should be used under medical supervision. Sorbitol is naturally present in dried fruits and contributes to the laxative effects of prunes. It was first discovered in 1872 in the fresh juice of mountain ash berries and is also found in fruits such as apples, plums, pears, cherries, dates, peaches, and apricots. In medical applications, sorbitol is used in bacterial culture media to differentiate pathogenic Escherichia coli O157:H7 from other E. coli strains, as the former typically cannot ferment sorbitol. Sorbitol is also used in combination with sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) to treat hyperkalemia by facilitating the removal of excess potassium ions. The resin exchanges sodium ions for potassium ions in the bowel, while sorbitol aids in the elimination process. However, the FDA has issued warnings about an increased risk of gastrointestinal necrosis with this combination. In healthcare, food, and cosmetics, sorbitol is frequently used as a humectant and thickener in modern cosmetic formulations, including mouthwash and toothpaste. It is also used in the production of transparent gels due to its high refractive index. Sorbitol is a common ingredient in sugar-free chewing gum and is used as a cryoprotectant additive in the manufacture of surimi, a refined fish paste. Additionally, it serves as a humectant in some cigarettes and as a sweetener and humectant in non-dietary food items such as cookies. Sorbitol has miscellaneous uses, including its application as a component in amateur solid rocket fuel when mixed with potassium nitrate. It is also identified as a potential key chemical intermediate for producing fuels from biomass resources. Carbohydrate fractions in biomass, such as cellulose, undergo hydrolysis and hydrogenation in the presence of metal catalysts to produce sorbitol. Complete reduction of sorbitol can yield alkanes like hexane, which can serve as biofuels. Hydrogen required for this reaction can be generated through aqueous-phase reforming of sorbitol, with five moles of sorbitol producing approximately one mole of hexane. When hydrogen is co-fed, no carbon dioxide is produced. Sorbitol is also used in yeast transformation protocols after electroporation to raise the osmolarity of the medium, aiding cell recovery. From a medical perspective, sorbitol is involved in the sorbitol-aldose reductase pathway, where aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol and galactose to galactitol. Excessive accumulation of sorbitol in retinal cells, lens cells, and Schwann cells can lead to cellular damage, resulting in complications such as retinopathy, cataracts, and peripheral neuropathy, respectively. Aldose reductase inhibitors are being investigated as potential treatments to prevent or delay these complications, which are commonly associated with long-term hyperglycemia in poorly controlled diabetes. These inhibitors may help prevent intracellular sorbitol accumulation and subsequent cellular damage. Adverse effects of sorbitol include its potential to exacerbate irritable bowel syndrome and similar gastrointestinal conditions, causing severe abdominal pain even with small amounts ingested. Sorbitol, when combined with sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS) for hyperkalemia treatment, has been associated with gastrointestinal complications such as bleeding, perforated colonic ulcers, ischemic colitis, and colonic necrosis, particularly in patients with uremia. Studies in rats have shown that uremic rats on a sorbitol enema regimen experienced significant colonic damage, while those on non-sorbitol regimens did not. Physicians are advised to exercise caution when using SPS-sorbitol combinations and to be aware of potential gastrointestinal side effects. In cases of overdose, consuming large amounts of sorbitol can lead to abdominal pain, flatulence, and diarrhea, ranging from mild to severe. For example, excessive consumption of sugar-free gum containing sorbitol has been reported to cause severe diarrhea and unintended weight loss. In one case, a woman consuming 20 grams of sorbitol daily lost 11 kilograms (24 pounds) over eight months, while another patient required hospitalization after consuming 30 grams daily.
